task_id.description: The ID of the background task to stop. Agent-team teammates and named background agents are also accepted by agent ID or name.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: WebFetch
tools.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead. claude.ai artifact links (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}) are published artifacts: read them with the Artifact tool (action "read"), not WebFetch or curl.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

url.description: The URL to fetch content from

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

offset.description: Character position in the page text to start reading from. Use it to read on through a page too long for one call, with the value the previous result gave.

tools.name: WebSearch
tools.description:
Search the web. Returns result blocks with titles and URLs. US-only.

- The current month is (provided in the conversation below) — use this when searching for recent information.
- `allowed_domains` / `blocked_domains` filter results.
- After answering from results, end with a "Sources:" list of the URLs you used as markdown links.

allowed_domains.description: Only include search results from these domains

blocked_domains.description: Never include search results from these domains

mode.description: "standard": the normal web search: quick and cheap; right for straightforward lookups (reference facts, official pages, documentation, well-known people, places and topics) and simple follow-up lookups. "extended": a thorough, fresh search at several times the cost and latency.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

tools.name: mcp__1a59c906-04da-521d-bda7-7f71b9f9e01c__batch
tools.description: Create a doc, or apply several operations to one doc atomically.

tools.name: mcp__1a59c906-04da-521d-bda7-7f71b9f9e01c__guide
tools.description: Docs guides: topic.instructions repeats the server instructions. Read it only if your client dropped them. Also topic.<name>, refusal.<code>. After a doc's birth → ["topic.index"].

items.description: topic.<name> (instructions, index, editing, tabs, comments, charts, chart-definition, diagram, uploads, sharing, skill) or refusal.<code>; several per call is fine.

tools.name: mcp__1a59c906-04da-521d-bda7-7f71b9f9e01c__update
tools.description: Edit a tab's contents, rename a doc or tab, or change a stored value.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a proposal you made with start_session (initiation "own_initiative" or "offer") that the user has not started.

Call this when it went stale: the work was done here after all (by you or the user), it turned out unnecessary, or you proposed a better-scoped replacement (propose the new one first, then dismiss the old task_id). A card the user answered has already left, "Do it here" included, so it needs no call.

task_id.description: The task_id the start_session proposal returned.

reason.description: Optional one-line reason the suggestion is no longer needed, e.g. "fixed in this session" or "superseded by task_ab12cd34".

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__hand_off_to_session
tools.description: Move the task you are in the middle of into its own session (a fork of this conversation plus your remaining plan) so you can answer the user now. Use it when a new user message about something else arrives mid-task — not for small corrections or when the user said to keep the work here. In a worktree the fork gets a fresh worktree, normally cut from your branch tip: commit first (uncommitted edits stay here). Bold title line and one sentence right before the call; after it, stop that task here and answer the new message — no recap.

title.description: Under 60 chars; names the task being moved.

remaining_plan.description: What is left to do: steps, files, what done looks like.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

title.description: Short noun-phrase title for the chapter (under 40 chars). Shown in the table of contents.

summary.description: Optional one-line summary of what this chapter covers. Shown on hover in the table of contents.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__read_widget_context
tools.description: Read context from an embedded interactive widget. Widgets are rendered alongside chat from prior tool calls and can be interacted with by the user. Call this when you need to know the current state of a widget.

tool_name.description: The name of the widget tool to get context for

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

scope.description: Required with items: "first_task", "continuation" or "new_task" (see the tool description). Omit on advance / done / start updates.

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

items.description: The whole plan, in order (1–12 steps); replaces the previous list.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields — recap and ask are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available now, or one your own work this turn made available; anything else is refused, and one that stops being available later is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and the other answers), so do not guess. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Fix 2 instead", "Not now": a button, not a sentence. A click sends it to you as the user's answer. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action (the app's own label is used).

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

input.content:
# Print hosts without a printer

Docker containers that run the real print-host software, for testing the app's
Moonraker and OctoPrint paths: connecting, API keys, status, and sending a
print. Only the printer boards are simulated. Bambu printers are covered by the
in-process fake instead ([Fake Bambu README](../../src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Testing/README.md)).

| Address | What answers | Key |
|---|---|---|
| `http://127.0.0.1:7130` | Moonraker on Klipper, trusts every address | none |
| `http://127.0.0.1:7131` | the same Klipper through a second Moonraker | needed; HTTP 401 without it |
| `http://127.0.0.1:5030` | OctoPrint 1.11.2 with its bundled virtual printer | needed; HTTP 403 without it |

Klipper's board is simulavr, an AVR simulator running Klipper's own firmware,
set up from [prind](https://github.com/mkuf/prind). OctoPrint's printer is its
[Virtual Printer](https://docs.octoprint.org/en/devel/bundledplugins/virtual_printer.html)
plugin, which acts like a Marlin printer on a serial port.

## Start and stop

Needs Docker (Docker Desktop on macOS and Windows).

```bash
docker compose -f tests/printer_hosts/docker-compose.yml up -d
```

The first start builds the simulavr image, which prind does not publish: about
6 minutes. Klipper reports `ready` some seconds after the containers start:

```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:7130/printer/info
```

Print the keys as shell exports (`JP_MOONRAKER_KEY`, `JP_OCTOPRINT_KEY`, and a
wrong one, `JP_BAD_KEY`):

```bash
eval "$(tests/printer_hosts/keys.sh)"
```

OctoPrint's key is fixed in `docker-compose.yml`. Moonraker makes its own key
on first start and keeps it until the volumes are removed. OctoPrint's web page
signs in as `admin` / `jusprin-test`.

```bash
docker compose -f tests/printer_hosts/docker-compose.yml down       # keeps keys and uploaded files
docker compose -f tests/printer_hosts/docker-compose.yml down -v    # back to a first start
```

The simulator uses one CPU core for as long as it runs, so stop the stack when
you are done.

## States worth testing

- **Ready, printing, paused, cancelled, complete:** send G-code with the app,
  or through the API (`/server/files/upload` with `print=true`,
  `/printer/print/pause`, `/printer/print/cancel`). Prints take their real
  time: the app's 20 mm cube on the generic Klipper printer runs about 10
  minutes.
- **Klipper in error behind a working Moonraker:** `docker compose … stop simulavr`.
  Start it again, then restart `klipper` (a `FIRMWARE_RESTART` cannot reset the
  simulated board).
- **Host offline:** stop the Moonraker or OctoPrint container.
- **Nothing listening:** any other port, such as `7139`.
- **Wrong host type:** OctoPrint at `7130` (Moonraker answers OctoPrint's API
  through its `[octoprint_compat]` section, so this connects), or Moonraker at
  `5030` (HTTP 404).

## The printer

`klipper/printer.cfg` matches the app's generic Klipper printer (MyKlipper 0.4
nozzle: 250 × 250 × 250, 0.4 mm nozzle, 1.75 mm filament) and defines the
`PRINT_START` and `PRINT_END` macros its start and end G-code call, so that
printer's G-code prints unchanged. simulavr's endstops always read as pressed
and its thermistors read about 103 °C, so homing sets the position without
moving, and M109/M190 set a temperature without waiting for it. Status reports
the target temperatures, but the measured ones stay near 103 °C.

## With the shell harness

`--print-host-check` takes a file of cases, one per line, and runs the app's
connection tool on each without a model:

```
moonraker http://127.0.0.1:7130
moonraker http://127.0.0.1:7131 JP_MOONRAKER_KEY
octoprint http://127.0.0.1:5030 JP_BAD_KEY
```

Export the keys first, as above.

## Versions

Every image is pinned. The simulavr build's `VERSION` must be the Klipper
commit of the `mkuf/klipper` tag (the part after `-g` in the tag), because
Klipper refuses a board built from different firmware. To move to newer
images, change both together, along with the prind commit in the build
context.

toolUseResult.originalFile:
# Print hosts without a printer

Docker containers that run the real print-host software, for testing the app's
Moonraker and OctoPrint paths: connecting, API keys, status, and sending a
print. Only the printer boards are simulated. Bambu printers are covered by the
in-process fake instead ([Fake Bambu README](../../src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Testing/README.md)).

| Address | What answers | Key |
|---|---|---|
| `http://127.0.0.1:7130` | Moonraker on Klipper, trusts every address | none |
| `http://127.0.0.1:7131` | the same Klipper through a second Moonraker | needed; HTTP 401 without it |
| `http://127.0.0.1:5030` | OctoPrint 1.11.2 with its bundled virtual printer | needed; HTTP 403 without it |

Klipper's board is simulavr, an AVR simulator running Klipper's own firmware,
set up from [prind](https://github.com/mkuf/prind). OctoPrint's printer is its
[Virtual Printer](https://docs.octoprint.org/en/devel/bundledplugins/virtual_printer.html)
plugin, which acts like a Marlin printer on a serial port.

## Start and stop

Needs Docker (Docker Desktop on macOS and Windows).

```bash
docker compose -f tests/printer_hosts/docker-compose.yml up -d
```

The first start builds the simulavr image, which prind does not publish: about
6 minutes. Klipper reports `ready` some seconds after the containers start:

```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:7130/printer/info
```

Print the keys as shell exports (`JP_MOONRAKER_KEY`, `JP_OCTOPRINT_KEY`, and a
wrong one, `JP_BAD_KEY`):

```bash
eval "$(tests/printer_hosts/keys.sh)"
```

OctoPrint's key is fixed in `docker-compose.yml`. Moonraker makes its own key
on first start and keeps it until the volumes are removed. OctoPrint's web page
signs in as `admin` / `jusprin-test`.

```bash
docker compose -f tests/printer_hosts/docker-compose.yml down       # keeps keys and uploaded files
docker compose -f tests/printer_hosts/docker-compose.yml down -v    # back to a first start
```

The simulator uses one CPU core for as long as it runs, so stop the stack when
you are done.

## States worth testing

- **Ready, printing, paused, cancelled, complete:** send G-code with the app,
  or through the API (`/server/files/upload` with `print=true`,
  `/printer/print/pause`, `/printer/print/cancel`). Prints take their real
  time: the app's 20 mm cube on the generic Klipper printer runs about 10
  minutes.
- **Klipper in error behind a working Moonraker:** `docker compose … stop simulavr`.
  Start it again, then restart `klipper` (a `FIRMWARE_RESTART` cannot reset the
  simulated board).
- **Host offline:** stop the Moonraker or OctoPrint container.
- **Nothing listening:** any other port, such as `7139`.
- **Wrong host type:** OctoPrint at `7130` (Moonraker answers OctoPrint's API
  through its `[octoprint_compat]` section, so this connects), or Moonraker at
  `5030` (HTTP 404).

## The printer

`klipper/printer.cfg` matches the app's generic Klipper printer (MyKlipper 0.4
nozzle: 250 × 250 × 250, 0.4 mm nozzle, 1.75 mm filament) and defines the
`PRINT_START` and `PRINT_END` macros its start and end G-code call, so that
printer's G-code prints unchanged. simulavr's endstops always read as pressed
and its thermistors read about 103 °C, so homing sets the position without
moving, and M109/M190 set a temperature without waiting for it. Status reports
the target temperatures, but the measured ones stay near 103 °C.

## With the shell harness

`--print-host-check` takes a file of cases, one per line, and runs the app's
connection tool on each without a model:

```
moonraker http://127.0.0.1:7130
moonraker http://127.0.0.1:7131 JP_MOONRAKER_KEY
octoprint http://127.0.0.1:5030 JP_BAD_KEY
```

Export the keys first, as above.

## Versions

Every image is pinned. The simulavr build's `VERSION` must be the Klipper
commit of the `mkuf/klipper` tag (the part after `-g` in the tag), because
Klipper refuses a board built from different firmware. To move to newer
images, change both together, along with the prind commit in the build
context.

# Fake Bambu printer (in-process)

Substitutes `FakeBambuAgent` for Bambu's closed network plugin so header menu,
Select Machine, and print can run without hardware. It is not a network fake:
MQTT, FTPS, and discovery are not implemented.

Moonraker and OctoPrint printers run against the real host software in Docker
([print hosts README](../../../../../tests/printer_hosts/README.md)). Do not add a Bambu network
fake unless asked.

This file is the operator guide for humans and AI agents.

## What success looks like

- Log: `switch_printer_agent: printer agent switched to jusprin-fake-bambu`
- Log: `set_selected_machine=FAKE001` and later `FakeBambuAgent: connected FAKE001`
- Printer chip shows `Bambu Lab A1 mini · 0.4` (nickname and nozzle only)
- Click the **printer** half of that chip. The **first menu row** is Idle,
  Printing, or Offline. Those words are never on the chip itself.

If the log says `moonraker` or `orca`, the fake is not in the path. Stop and
fix the preset; do not patch UI gates.

## Turn it on

Quit JusPrin first. The app rewrites `JusPrin2.conf` on exit.

`JusPrin2.conf` is JSON. Under the scratch datadir:

```json
"jusprin": { "fake_printer": true }
```

JSON `true` is what the app stores; `get("jusprin", "fake_printer")` reads as
the string `"true"`. An INI `[jusprin]` block is ignored.

Keep a **Bambu Lab printer** selected: a real system preset, typically
`Bambu Lab A1 mini 0.4 nozzle`, or a named printer that inherits one.
`is_bbl_vendor()` must be true; it reads the inherited `printer_model`, so
either works. An embedded 3mf preset named
`Bambu Lab A1 mini 0.4 nozzle(Tape_4_3MF.3mf)` is not enough; the agent stays
`orca`.

**Add a printer…** in the printer menu installs the system preset and saves it
as a named printer (a user profile such as `Bambu Lab A1 mini`), which is what
Home lists. Alternatively copy `Resources/profiles/BBL` into
`<datadir>/system/` and add the A1 mini model to the `models` array in
`JusPrin2.conf`, then select the system preset. Opening
`~/Downloads/Tape_4_3MF.3mf` only helps after that vendor is installed.

Launch a **scratch** `--datadir`. Do not point fake mode at the everyday
config. JusPrin turns `single_instance` on at every start; its instance lock
lives in the data directory, so a scratch `--datadir` runs as its own instance
beside another JusPrin. Do not pass `--no-single-instance`; Boost rejects it.

The fake emulates printer type `N1` (A1 mini). Select Machine lists it as
**JusPrin Fake A1 mini (LAN)**.

For an MCP client, the shell harness does all of this in its own datadir:
`shell_integration_harness --manual-mcp <dir> --fake-printer` saves a
**Fake A1 mini** printer, connects it to the fake and selects it before it
prints `HARNESS MCP FIXTURE READY`. Edits to the conf would not survive: the
fixture rewrites it at startup.

## Drive state

Write `<datadir>/jusprin/fake_printer.json` (create `jusprin/` if needed). The
fake rereads it about once a second.

```json
{"state":"printing","progress":0.4,"nozzle":210,"bed":60,"offline":false}
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `state` | `idle`, `heating`/`prepare`, `printing`/`running`, `pause`, `finished`, `failed` |
| `progress` | 0–1, mapped to `mc_percent` |
| `nozzle`, `bed` | °C |
| `offline` | `true` stops `push_status`; after ~30 s the menu first row is Offline |
| `spools` | loaded AMS spools; see below. Absent leaves whatever was last set |
| `send_fails` | `true` makes the next print or storage upload fail as an upload failure (read at the moment of Send), so OrcaSlicer's send dialog shows its error and reports no success |
| `connect_fails` | a code such as `"5"` (or `true`, which is `"5"`) makes every connect report `ConnectStatusFailed` with that code to the app, as the plug-in does for a printer that refuses; upstream reads `"5"` as a wrong access code and erases the saved one. Nothing connects while it is set. Tests can also call `fail_next_connect(code)` on the agent for one connect |

No `spools` (or an empty array) reports no AMS at all, same as before this
field existed. A non-empty array reports one AMS unit (id `"0"`) with one
tray per spool, up to 4:

```json
{"spools": [{"subBrands": "PLA Matte", "trayType": "PLA", "colour": "5F7D4FFF"}]}
```

`subBrands` is what `PrinterDiscovery.cpp` reads back as the spool's name
when set (ahead of `trayType`), so it is the field worth setting for a
saved/network-printer card or receipt to show something. `trayType` is the
spool's material (Home's Loaded row names it); the fake sends it beside a
`tray_info_idx`, since upstream ignores a type that arrives without one.
`filamentId` sets that id (`"GFA01"` is Bambu PLA Matte); left out, the
id is empty, and Orca's filament sync skips the tray. `colour` is optional: a spool without it reports no colour, and Home
draws no swatch for it.

Delete the file, or set `"offline": false` and `"state":"idle"`, to return to Idle.

## Print

Slice, then Print (or Cmd+Shift+G on macOS). Send completes without a printer.
The log records `FakeBambuAgent: start_local_print file=...`.

If the control file is present, that file wins: send still succeeds, but the
menu stays on the file's state. Remove the file if you want the canned printing
scenario after send.

## Isolate a running app (agents)

Another JusPrin may already be open. Do not send keys or clicks to it.

On macOS both processes are often named `OrcaSlicer`. Target by unix pid or by
a unique `CFBundleIdentifier` on a ditto'd `.app` (then ad-hoc `codesign`).
`osascript` `unix id` filters can match the wrong process; prefer
`AXUIElementCreateApplication(pid)` or the unique bundle id.

Keyboard events posted to the pid work while the Mac is locked; mouse events
posted that way do not. Menus only open when that app is frontmost. The printer
half of the chip is a wx control (`SetName("Printer")`) and often has no AX
title; click by coordinates after a screenshot, or use the documented shortcut
for Print.

Logs: `<datadir>/log/debug_*.log`. This machine's default `grep` may be ugrep;
use `/usr/bin/grep -a` on app logs.

## A real printer, no model

The printer tools are not exposed over MCP, so `probe.call` cannot reach them.
`shell_integration_harness --printer-network-check <dir> <address> <version>`
drives them with a scripted stand-in for the model, on Bambu's real plug-in:
copy `plugins/` from a data folder that has it into `<dir>` first, and pass the
version in its `libbambu_networking_<version>.dylib` name. It expects a P1S in
cloud mode at `<address>`, prints each tool result and note as
`HARNESS NETWORK` lines, and sends the printer nothing. `--simulate-announce` after
the version hands the app that announcement itself 25 seconds in, for when no
printer is on; it tests everything after the plug-in, not the plug-in. Printers announce on UDP
2021. While another program holds that port the plug-in hears nothing, and
`printer_connection_status` reports `port_taken`, so quit whatever
`lsof -nP -iUDP:2021` names first. The plug-in takes the port only as the app
starts, so once that program lets go the status reports `not_listening` until a
restart. Holding the port from a small script is how to test both states.

`--printer-connect-skill <dir> <address> <version>` runs the same chats for
the connection skill; pass `none` as the version to run without the plug-in.
`--open-issue` after the version also calls `issue_report_open`, which opens
the default browser on a filled-in GitHub issue page. Nothing is filed unless
someone presses Submit there, so close the tab. That run keeps its data
folder; the link is in `log/debug_*.log` under "opening an issue page".

## Unit tests

`jusprin_fake_bambu_tests` (Catch2, GUI build). They cover announce JSON,
control-file parsing, and agent id. They do not start the heartbeat unless the
test sets `set_queue_on_main_fn`.

## Agent id

Registered as `jusprin-fake-bambu`. `GUI_App::switch_printer_agent` uses that
id in place of `bbl` when fake mode is on. No other upstream file is involved.

 && apt install -y cmake \

COPY requirements-prind.txt .
RUN python -m venv venv \
 && venv/bin/pip install -r requirements-prind.txt
ARG REPO=https://github.com/Klipper3d/klipper
ARG VERSION=master
RUN git clone ${REPO} klipper \
 && cd klipper \
 && git checkout ${VERSION} \
 && echo -n $(git describe --tags)-prind > klippy/.version \
 && rm -rf .git

 && venv/bin/python -m compileall klipper/klippy \
 && venv/bin/python klipper/klippy/chelper/__init__.py
FROM python:3.12-slim-trixie AS run

RUN groupadd klipper --gid 1000 \
 && useradd klipper --uid 1000 --gid klipper \
 && usermod klipper --append --groups dialout \
 && usermod klipper --append --groups tty
RUN mkdir -p printer_data/run printer_data/gcodes printer_data/logs printer_data/config \

# The Klipper printer's board: Klipper's AVR firmware running in simulavr.
#
# This is prind's build-simulavr stage (docker/klipper/Dockerfile at
# github.com/mkuf/prind 6f7690117230f4128101f0b0d2d72bf8a37cae8a), with two
# changes prind's file has no switch for:
# - It starts from prind's published tools image for the klipper service's
#   tag, which holds that tag's Klipper source, so the firmware always matches
#   the Klipper that talks to it.
# - simulavr is built with -O2. prind's README suggests this when Klipper
#   times out; the default debug build here ran at about a fifth of real time,
#   so prints took about five times their estimate.
# config.simulavr is prind's file of the same name.
ARG KLIPPER_TAG
FROM mkuf/klipper:${KLIPPER_TAG}-tools

RUN apt update \
 && apt install -y git cmake swig python3-dev python3-setuptools \
 && apt clean

WORKDIR /opt/klipper
COPY config.simulavr .config
RUN make

WORKDIR /opt
RUN mkdir run \
 && groupadd simulavr --gid 1000 \
 && useradd simulavr --uid 1000 --gid simulavr \
 && usermod simulavr --append --groups dialout

ENV CXXFLAGS="-O2"
RUN git clone git://git.savannah.nongnu.org/simulavr.git \
 && cd simulavr \
 && git checkout release-1.1.0 \
 && make python \
 && make build \
 && chown -R simulavr:simulavr /opt/simulavr

USER simulavr
ENV PYTHONPATH=/opt/simulavr/build/pysimulavr/
VOLUME ["/opt/printer_data/run"]
ENTRYPOINT ["klipper/scripts/avrsim.py"]
CMD ["-p", "/opt/printer_data/run/simulavr.tty", "/opt/klipper/out/klipper.elf"]

# Print hosts for testing without a printer: a Klipper printer behind two
# Moonrakers (one open, one that wants an API key) and an OctoPrint with its
# built-in virtual printer. All of it is the real software; only the printer
# boards are simulated. See README.md.
name: jusprin-printer-hosts

services:
  # The Klipper printer's board, simulated by simulavr. prind builds this image
  # but does not publish it, so the first `up` builds it (about 6 minutes).
  # VERSION is the Klipper commit of the klipper image below; the board's
  # firmware and Klipper must match.
  simulavr:
    image: jusprin-test-simulavr:0cee841e3
    build:
      context: https://github.com/mkuf/prind.git#6f7690117230f4128101f0b0d2d72bf8a37cae8a:docker/klipper
      target: build-simulavr
      args:
        VERSION: 0cee841e31d701595b3e509a0b502f6e320f52a8
    restart: unless-stopped
    # The simulated serial port is a pty under /dev/pts; Klipper opens it
    # through a link in the shared run volume, so both see the same /dev.
    privileged: true
    volumes:
      - /dev:/dev
      - run:/opt/printer_data/run

  klipper:
    image: mkuf/klipper:v0.13.0-820-g0cee841e3
    restart: unless-stopped
    privileged: true
    depends_on: [simulavr]
    command: >
      -I printer_data/run/klipper.tty
      -a printer_data/run/klipper.sock
      printer_data/config/printer.cfg
      -l printer_data/logs/klippy.log
    volumes:
      - /dev:/dev
      - ./klipper/printer.cfg:/opt/printer_data/config/printer.cfg:ro
      - run:/opt/printer_data/run
      - gcodes:/opt/printer_data/gcodes
      - klipper-logs:/opt/printer_data/logs

  # Answers without a key, like a printer on a home network that trusts it.
  moonraker-open:
    image: mkuf/moonraker:v0.11.0-4-gb559b9a
    restart: unless-stopped
    depends_on: [klipper]
    ports:
      - "7130:7125"
    volumes:
      - ./moonraker/open.conf:/opt/printer_data/config/moonraker.conf:ro
      - run:/opt/printer_data/run
      - gcodes:/opt/printer_data/gcodes
      - moonraker-open-db:/opt/printer_data/database

  # Same printer, but every request from outside the container needs the API
  # key (HTTP 401 without it). ./keys.sh prints the key.
  moonraker-key:
    image: mkuf/moonraker:v0.11.0-4-gb559b9a
    restart: unless-stopped
    depends_on: [klipper]
    ports:
      - "7131:7125"
    volumes:
      - ./moonraker/key.conf:/opt/printer_data/config/moonraker.conf:ro
      - run:/opt/printer_data/run
      - gcodes:/opt/printer_data/gcodes
      - moonraker-key-db:/opt/printer_data/database

  # OctoPrint with its bundled virtual printer connected; every request needs
  # the API key (HTTP 403 without it).
  octoprint:
    image: octoprint/octoprint:1.11.2-minimal
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "5030:5000"
    environment:
      OCTOPRINT_API_KEY: JUSPRINTESTOCTOPRINTKEY000000000
    entrypoint: ["sh", "/seed/start.sh"]
    volumes:
      - ./octoprint:/seed:ro
      - octoprint-data:/octoprint

volumes:
  run:
  gcodes:
  klipper-logs:
  moonraker-open-db:
  moonraker-key-db:
  octoprint-data:

# The Klipper printer's board: Klipper's AVR firmware running in simulavr.
#
# This is prind's build-simulavr stage (docker/klipper/Dockerfile at
# github.com/mkuf/prind 6f7690117230f4128101f0b0d2d72bf8a37cae8a), with two
# changes prind's file has no switch for:
# - It starts from prind's published tools image for the klipper service's
#   tag, which holds that tag's Klipper source, so the firmware always matches
#   the Klipper that talks to it.
# - simulavr is built with -O2. prind's README suggests this when Klipper
#   times out; the default debug build here ran at about a fifth of real time,
#   so prints took about five times their estimate.
# config.simulavr is prind's file of the same name.
ARG KLIPPER_TAG
FROM mkuf/klipper:${KLIPPER_TAG}-tools

RUN apt update \
 && apt install -y git cmake swig python3-dev python3-setuptools \
 && apt clean

WORKDIR /opt/klipper
COPY config.simulavr .config
RUN make

WORKDIR /opt
RUN mkdir run \
 && groupadd simulavr --gid 1000 \
 && useradd simulavr --uid 1000 --gid simulavr \
 && usermod simulavr --append --groups dialout

ENV CXXFLAGS="-O2"
RUN git clone git://git.savannah.nongnu.org/simulavr.git \
 && cd simulavr \
 && git checkout release-1.1.0 \
 && make python \
 && make build \
 && chown -R simulavr:simulavr /opt/simulavr

USER simulavr
ENV PYTHONPATH=/opt/simulavr/build/pysimulavr/
VOLUME ["/opt/printer_data/run"]
ENTRYPOINT ["klipper/scripts/avrsim.py"]
CMD ["-p", "/opt/printer_data/run/simulavr.tty", "/opt/klipper/out/klipper.elf"]

# Print hosts without a printer

Docker containers that run the real print-host software, for testing the app's
Moonraker and OctoPrint paths: connecting, API keys, status, and sending a
print. Only the printer boards are simulated. Bambu printers are covered by the
in-process fake instead ([Fake Bambu README](../../src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Testing/README.md)).

| Address | What answers | Key |
|---|---|---|
| `http://127.0.0.1:7130` | Moonraker on Klipper, trusts every address | none |
| `http://127.0.0.1:7131` | the same Klipper through a second Moonraker | needed; HTTP 401 without it |
| `http://127.0.0.1:5030` | OctoPrint 1.11.2 with its bundled virtual printer | needed; HTTP 403 without it |

Klipper's board is simulavr, an AVR simulator running Klipper's own firmware,
set up from [prind](https://github.com/mkuf/prind). OctoPrint's printer is its
[Virtual Printer](https://docs.octoprint.org/en/devel/bundledplugins/virtual_printer.html)
plugin, which acts like a Marlin printer on a serial port.

## Start and stop

Needs Docker (Docker Desktop on macOS and Windows).

```bash
docker compose -f tests/printer_hosts/docker-compose.yml up -d
```

The first start builds the simulavr image, which prind does not publish: about
6 minutes. Klipper reports `ready` some seconds after the containers start:

```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:7130/printer/info
```

Print the keys as shell exports (`JP_MOONRAKER_KEY`, `JP_OCTOPRINT_KEY`, and a
wrong one, `JP_BAD_KEY`):

```bash
eval "$(tests/printer_hosts/keys.sh)"
```

OctoPrint's key is fixed in `docker-compose.yml`. Moonraker makes its own key
on first start and keeps it until the volumes are removed. OctoPrint's web page
signs in as `admin` / `jusprin-test`.

```bash
docker compose -f tests/printer_hosts/docker-compose.yml down       # keeps keys and uploaded files
docker compose -f tests/printer_hosts/docker-compose.yml down -v    # back to a first start
```

The simulator uses one CPU core for as long as it runs, so stop the stack when
you are done.

## States worth testing

- **Ready, printing, paused, cancelled, complete:** send G-code with the app,
  or through the API (`/server/files/upload` with `print=true`,
  `/printer/print/pause`, `/printer/print/cancel`). Prints take their real
  time: the app's 20 mm cube on the generic Klipper printer runs about 10
  minutes.
- **Klipper in error behind a working Moonraker:** `docker compose … stop simulavr`.
  Start it again, then restart `klipper` (a `FIRMWARE_RESTART` cannot reset the
  simulated board).
- **Host offline:** stop the Moonraker or OctoPrint container.
- **Nothing listening:** any other port, such as `7139`.
- **Wrong host type:** OctoPrint at `7130` (Moonraker answers OctoPrint's API
  through its `[octoprint_compat]` section, so this connects), or Moonraker at
  `5030` (HTTP 404).

## The printer

`klipper/printer.cfg` matches the app's generic Klipper printer (MyKlipper 0.4
nozzle: 250 × 250 × 250, 0.4 mm nozzle, 1.75 mm filament) and defines the
`PRINT_START` and `PRINT_END` macros its start and end G-code call, so that
printer's G-code prints unchanged. simulavr's endstops always read as pressed
and its thermistors read about 103 °C, so homing sets the position without
moving, and M109/M190 set a temperature without waiting for it. Status reports
the target temperatures, but the measured ones stay near 103 °C.

## With the shell harness

`--print-host-check` takes a file of cases, one per line, and runs the app's
connection tool on each without a model:

```
moonraker http://127.0.0.1:7130
moonraker http://127.0.0.1:7131 JP_MOONRAKER_KEY
octoprint http://127.0.0.1:5030 JP_BAD_KEY
```

Export the keys first, as above.

## Versions

Every image is pinned. The simulavr build's `VERSION` must be the Klipper
commit of the `mkuf/klipper` tag (the part after `-g` in the tag): Klipper
expects its board's firmware to come from the same Klipper version. To move to newer
images, change both together, along with the prind commit in the build
context.

## Start and stop

Needs Docker (Docker Desktop on macOS and Windows).

```bash
docker compose -f tests/printer_hosts/docker-compose.yml up -d
```

The first start builds the simulavr image, which nobody publishes
([simulavr/Dockerfile](simulavr/Dockerfile)): a few minutes, most of it
downloading prind's 1.6 GB Klipper tools image. Klipper reports `ready` some
seconds after the containers start:

```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:7130/printer/info
```

Print the keys as shell exports (`JP_MOONRAKER_KEY`, `JP_OCTOPRINT_KEY`, and a
wrong one, `JP_BAD_KEY`):

```bash
eval "$(tests/printer_hosts/keys.sh)"
```

OctoPrint's key is fixed in `docker-compose.yml`. Moonraker makes its own key
on first start and keeps it until the volumes are removed. OctoPrint's web page
signs in as `admin` / `jusprin-test`.

```bash
docker compose -f tests/printer_hosts/docker-compose.yml down       # keeps keys and uploaded files
docker compose -f tests/printer_hosts/docker-compose.yml down -v    # back to a first start
```

The simulator uses one CPU core for as long as it runs, so stop the stack when
you are done.

## States worth testing

- **Ready, printing, paused, cancelled, complete:** send G-code with the app,
  or through the API (`/server/files/upload` with `print=true`,
  `/printer/print/pause`, `/printer/print/cancel`). Prints take their real
  time: the app's 20 mm cube on the generic Klipper printer runs about 10
  minutes.
- **Klipper in error behind a working Moonraker:** `docker compose … stop simulavr`.
  Start it again, then restart `klipper` (a `FIRMWARE_RESTART` cannot reset the
  simulated board).
- **Host offline:** stop the Moonraker or OctoPrint container.
- **Nothing listening:** any other port, such as `7139`.
- **Wrong host type:** OctoPrint at `7130` (Moonraker answers OctoPrint's API
  through its `[octoprint_compat]` section, so this connects), or Moonraker at
  `5030` (HTTP 404).

## The printer

`klipper/printer.cfg` matches the app's generic Klipper printer (MyKlipper 0.4
nozzle: 250 × 250 × 250, 0.4 mm nozzle, 1.75 mm filament) and defines the
`PRINT_START` and `PRINT_END` macros its start and end G-code call, so that
printer's G-code prints unchanged. simulavr's endstops always read as pressed
and its thermistors read about 103 °C, so homing sets the position without
moving, and M109/M190 set a temperature without waiting for it. Status reports
the target temperatures, but the measured ones stay near 103 °C.

## With the shell harness

`--print-host-check` takes a file of cases, one per line, and runs the app's
connection tool on each without a model:

```
moonraker http://127.0.0.1:7130
moonraker http://127.0.0.1:7131 JP_MOONRAKER_KEY
octoprint http://127.0.0.1:5030 JP_BAD_KEY
```

Export the keys first, as above.

## Versions

Every image is pinned. The simulavr build's `VERSION` must be the Klipper
commit of the `mkuf/klipper` tag (the part after `-g` in the tag): Klipper
expects its board's firmware to come from the same Klipper version. To move to newer
images, change both together, along with the prind commit in the build
context.

# The Klipper printer's board: Klipper's AVR firmware running in simulavr.
#
# This is prind's build-simulavr stage (docker/klipper/Dockerfile at
# github.com/mkuf/prind 6f7690117230f4128101f0b0d2d72bf8a37cae8a), with two
# changes prind's file has no switch for:
# - It starts from prind's published tools image for the klipper service's
#   tag, which holds that tag's Klipper source, so the firmware always matches
#   the Klipper that talks to it.
# - simulavr is built with -O2. prind's README suggests this when Klipper
#   times out; the default debug build here ran at about a fifth of real time,
#   so prints took about five times their estimate.
# config.simulavr is prind's file of the same name.
ARG KLIPPER_TAG
FROM mkuf/klipper:${KLIPPER_TAG}-tools

RUN apt update \
 && apt install -y git cmake swig python3-dev python3-setuptools \
 && apt clean

WORKDIR /opt/klipper
COPY config.simulavr .config
# olddefconfig fills in options newer than config.simulavr (such as
# CONFIG_AVR_BUILD_MCU). make alone skips it when the copied file looks newer
# than Klipper's Kconfig files, and the build then fails on an empty -mmcu=.
RUN make olddefconfig \
 && make

WORKDIR /opt
RUN mkdir run \
 && groupadd simulavr --gid 1000 \
 && useradd simulavr --uid 1000 --gid simulavr \
 && usermod simulavr --append --groups dialout

ENV CXXFLAGS="-O2"
RUN git clone git://git.savannah.nongnu.org/simulavr.git \
 && cd simulavr \
 && git checkout release-1.1.0 \
 && make python \
 && make build \
 && chown -R simulavr:simulavr /opt/simulavr

USER simulavr
ENV PYTHONPATH=/opt/simulavr/build/pysimulavr/
VOLUME ["/opt/printer_data/run"]
ENTRYPOINT ["klipper/scripts/avrsim.py"]
CMD ["-p", "/opt/printer_data/run/simulavr.tty", "/opt/klipper/out/klipper.elf"]

content.text:
Yes. For testing printer connections the simulators are ready now, and all five containers are running on your Mac. I already ran the app's own connection tool against them through the shell harness's `--print-host-check`, with no model involved. All 11 cases behaved like real hosts, with no failed checks:

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| Moonraker that needs no key, `http://127.0.0.1:7130` (also tried without `http://`) | verified, "Klipper's state as ready" |
| Moonraker that needs a key, `http://127.0.0.1:7131`, with no key or a wrong key | refused with HTTP 401, and the key form opens |
| Same Moonraker with the right key typed into the form | verified |
| OctoPrint, `http://127.0.0.1:5030`, with no key or a wrong key | refused with HTTP 403, and the key form opens |
| Same OctoPrint with the right key | verified |
| OctoPrint chosen as the type, but at the Moonraker address | verified. Moonraker answers OctoPrint's API, which is real Moonraker behaviour |
| Moonraker chosen as the type, but at the OctoPrint address | failed with HTTP 404 |
| Nothing listening at that port (`7139`) | failed, "Connection refused" |

To get the keys for typing into the app's form, run this from the repo root. It prints `JP_MOONRAKER_KEY`, `JP_OCTOPRINT_KEY` and a deliberately wrong `JP_BAD_KEY`:

```bash
tests/printer_hosts/keys.sh
```

OctoPrint's key is always `JUSPRINTESTOCTOPRINTKEY000000000`. Its web page is at `http://127.0.0.1:5030`, signed in as `admin` / `jusprin-test`.

To start the stack again later:

```bash
docker compose -f tests/printer_hosts/docker-compose.yml up -d
```

**What's still being worked on.** The connection part is done. The part still being tuned is long prints on the simulated Klipper board:
- Run at full speed, the simulator fell behind on busy moves after about 90 seconds and Klipper stopped with "Timer too close". An 8 MHz board did the same.
- I'm now running it at half speed. The app's 20 mm cube is 65% done after about 14 minutes with no errors, so a print takes about twice its estimate.
- OctoPrint's virtual printer prints with no tuning.

None of this affects connecting, checking status, or starting a print.

**Not done yet:**
- Confirm the half-speed print finishes, and update the README and the simulator Dockerfile's comment to match.
- Check that stopping the simulator container puts Klipper into its error state, as the README says.
- Nothing is committed. The new files are under `tests/printer_hosts/`, plus one-line pointers in `AGENTS.md`, `agent-docs/jusprin/README.md`, `agent-docs/jusprin/engineering-method.md` and `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Testing/README.md`.

Earlier containers from another session are also still running: `jp-moonraker` on 7125, `jp-moonraker-open` on 7126, and Mainsail on 8081 and 8082. Use the new ports so you're testing these simulators, not those.

toolUseResult.originalFile:
# The Klipper printer's board: Klipper's AVR firmware running in simulavr.
#
# This is prind's build-simulavr stage (docker/klipper/Dockerfile at
# github.com/mkuf/prind 6f7690117230f4128101f0b0d2d72bf8a37cae8a), changed
# where prind's file has no switch:
# - It starts from prind's published tools image for the klipper service's
#   tag, which holds that tag's Klipper source, so the firmware always matches
#   the Klipper that talks to it.
# - The simulated board must keep real time. Unpaced, simulavr runs the board
#   as fast as one core allows: prind's debug build managed about a fifth of
#   its 16 MHz (prints took five times their estimate), and an -O2 build just
#   under 16 MHz, where it fell behind on busy moves and Klipper shut down
#   with "Timer too close". So simulavr is built with -O2 (as prind's README
#   suggests), the board runs at 8 MHz, and avrsim.py paces it to real time.
# config.simulavr is prind's file of the same name, with the clock set to
# 8 MHz.
ARG KLIPPER_TAG
FROM mkuf/klipper:${KLIPPER_TAG}-tools

RUN apt update \
 && apt install -y git cmake swig python3-dev python3-setuptools \
 && apt clean

WORKDIR /opt/klipper
COPY config.simulavr .config
# olddefconfig fills in options newer than config.simulavr (such as
# CONFIG_AVR_BUILD_MCU). make alone skips it when the copied file looks newer
# than Klipper's Kconfig files, and the build then fails on an empty -mmcu=.
RUN make olddefconfig \
 && make

WORKDIR /opt
RUN mkdir run \
 && groupadd simulavr --gid 1000 \
 && useradd simulavr --uid 1000 --gid simulavr \
 && usermod simulavr --append --groups dialout

ENV CXXFLAGS="-O2"
RUN git clone git://git.savannah.nongnu.org/simulavr.git \
 && cd simulavr \
 && git checkout release-1.1.0 \
 && make python \
 && make build \
 && chown -R simulavr:simulavr /opt/simulavr

USER simulavr
ENV PYTHONPATH=/opt/simulavr/build/pysimulavr/
VOLUME ["/opt/printer_data/run"]
ENTRYPOINT ["klipper/scripts/avrsim.py"]
CMD ["-r", "0.5", "-p", "/opt/printer_data/run/simulavr.tty", "/opt/klipper/out/klipper.elf"]

# Print hosts without a printer

Docker containers that run the real print-host software, for testing the app's
Moonraker and OctoPrint paths: connecting, API keys, status, and sending a
print. Only the printer boards are simulated. Bambu printers are covered by the
in-process fake instead ([Fake Bambu README](../../src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Testing/README.md)).

| Address | What answers | Key |
|---|---|---|
| `http://127.0.0.1:7130` | Moonraker on Klipper, trusts every address | none |
| `http://127.0.0.1:7131` | the same Klipper through a second Moonraker | needed; HTTP 401 without it |
| `http://127.0.0.1:5030` | OctoPrint 1.11.2 with its bundled virtual printer | needed; HTTP 403 without it |

Klipper's board is simulavr, an AVR simulator running Klipper's own firmware,
set up from [prind](https://github.com/mkuf/prind). OctoPrint's printer is its
[Virtual Printer](https://docs.octoprint.org/en/devel/bundledplugins/virtual_printer.html)
plugin, which acts like a Marlin printer on a serial port.

## Start and stop

Needs Docker (Docker Desktop on macOS and Windows).

```bash
docker compose -f tests/printer_hosts/docker-compose.yml up -d
```

The first start builds the simulavr image, which nobody publishes
([simulavr/Dockerfile](simulavr/Dockerfile)): a few minutes, most of it
downloading prind's Klipper tools image (1.6 GB to download, about 5.5 GB on
disk with the built image). Klipper reports `ready` some
seconds after the containers start:

```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:7130/printer/info
```

Print the keys as shell exports (`JP_MOONRAKER_KEY`, `JP_OCTOPRINT_KEY`, and a
wrong one, `JP_BAD_KEY`):

```bash
eval "$(tests/printer_hosts/keys.sh)"
```

OctoPrint's key is fixed in `docker-compose.yml`. Moonraker makes its own key
on first start and keeps it until the volumes are removed. OctoPrint's web page
signs in as `admin` / `jusprin-test`.

```bash
docker compose -f tests/printer_hosts/docker-compose.yml down       # keeps keys and uploaded files
docker compose -f tests/printer_hosts/docker-compose.yml down -v    # back to a first start
```

The simulator uses one CPU core for as long as it runs, so stop the stack when
you are done.

## States worth testing

- **Ready, printing, paused, cancelled, complete:** send G-code with the app,
  or through the API (`/server/files/upload` with `print=true`,
  `/printer/print/pause`, `/printer/print/cancel`). Prints take their real
  time: the app's 20 mm cube on the generic Klipper printer runs about 10
  minutes.
- **Klipper in error behind a working Moonraker:** `docker compose … stop simulavr`.
  Start it again, then restart `klipper` (a `FIRMWARE_RESTART` cannot reset the
  simulated board).
- **Host offline:** stop the Moonraker or OctoPrint container.
- **Nothing listening:** any other port, such as `7139`.
- **Wrong host type:** OctoPrint at `7130` (Moonraker answers OctoPrint's API
  through its `[octoprint_compat]` section, so this connects), or Moonraker at
  `5030` (HTTP 404).

## The printer

`klipper/printer.cfg` matches the app's generic Klipper printer (MyKlipper 0.4
nozzle: 250 × 250 × 250, 0.4 mm nozzle, 1.75 mm filament) and defines the
`PRINT_START` and `PRINT_END` macros its start and end G-code call, so that
printer's G-code prints unchanged. simulavr's endstops always read as pressed
and its thermistors read about 103 °C, so homing sets the position without
moving, and M109/M190 set a temperature without waiting for it. Status reports
the target temperatures, but the measured ones stay near 103 °C.

## With the shell harness

`--print-host-check` takes a file of cases, one per line, and runs the app's
connection tool on each without a model:

```
moonraker http://127.0.0.1:7130
moonraker http://127.0.0.1:7131 JP_MOONRAKER_KEY
octoprint http://127.0.0.1:5030 JP_BAD_KEY
```

Export the keys first, as above.

## Versions

Every image is pinned. `KLIPPER_TAG` in [.env](.env) picks the
`mkuf/klipper` tag for both Klipper and the simulated board, whose firmware is
built from that tag's `-tools` image, so the two always match. After changing
it, rebuild with `docker compose … build simulavr`.

```

The simulated board uses most of a CPU core for as long as it runs, so stop the
stack when you are done.

## Connecting a printer in the app

Use a printer that is not made by Bambu Lab, such as the generic Klipper
printer, and give the app an address from the table above, with
Moonraker or OctoPrint as the host type. When the app asks for an API key, type
the one `keys.sh` prints, a wrong one, or none, depending on the case. Each
address answers the way a real host does:

| Address and key | What the app's connection test gets |
|---|---|
| `7130`, no key | accepted; Klipper is ready |
| `7131` or `5030`, no key or a wrong key | refused (HTTP 401 or 403), so the app asks for a key |
| `7131` or `5030`, the right key | accepted |

## States worth testing

- **Ready, printing, paused, cancelled, complete:** send G-code with the app,
  or through the API (`/server/files/upload` with `print=true`,
  `/printer/print/pause`, `/printer/print/cancel`). The simulated Klipper
  board runs at half speed (see [simulavr/Dockerfile](simulavr/Dockerfile)),
  so its prints take twice their estimate: the app's 20 mm cube on the
  generic Klipper printer, estimated at 10 minutes, takes about 20.
  OctoPrint's virtual printer keeps its own pace.
- **Klipper in error behind a working Moonraker:** `docker compose … stop simulavr`.
  Start it again, then restart `klipper` (a `FIRMWARE_RESTART` cannot reset the
  simulated board).
- **Host offline:** stop the Moonraker or OctoPrint container.
- **Nothing listening:** any other port, such as `7139`.
- **Wrong host type:** OctoPrint at `7130` (Moonraker answers OctoPrint's API
  through its `[octoprint_compat]` section, so this connects), or Moonraker at
  `5030` (HTTP 404).

## The printer

`klipper/printer.cfg` matches the app's generic Klipper printer (MyKlipper 0.4
nozzle: 250 × 250 × 250, 0.4 mm nozzle, 1.75 mm filament) and defines the
`PRINT_START` and `PRINT_END` macros its start and end G-code call, so that
printer's G-code prints unchanged. simulavr's endstops always read as pressed
and its thermistors read about 103 °C, so homing sets the position without
moving, and M109/M190 set a temperature without waiting for it. Status reports
the target temperatures, but the measured ones stay near 103 °C.

## With the shell harness

`--print-host-check` takes a file of cases, one per line, and runs the app's
connection tool on each without a model:

```
moonraker http://127.0.0.1:7130
moonraker http://127.0.0.1:7131 JP_MOONRAKER_KEY
octoprint http://127.0.0.1:5030 JP_BAD_KEY
```

Export the keys first, as above.

## Versions

Every image is pinned. `KLIPPER_TAG` in [.env](.env) picks the
`mkuf/klipper` tag for both Klipper and the simulated board, whose firmware is
built from that tag's `-tools` image, so the two always match. After changing
it, rebuild with `docker compose … build simulavr`.

Add Docker print hosts for testing Moonraker and OctoPrint without a printer

tests/printer_hosts/docker-compose.yml starts the real host software with
simulated printer boards:

- 127.0.0.1:7130: Moonraker on Klipper, trusting every address (no key).

  key (HTTP 401 without it).

  needs its API key (HTTP 403 without it).

prind's published tools image for the pinned Klipper tag so the firmware
always matches. Unpaced, simulavr fell behind on busy moves and Klipper shut
down with "Timer too close", so the board is built with -O2 and paced to half
of real time. printer.cfg matches the generic Klipper printer (MyKlipper 0.4
nozzle), works around simulavr's always-pressed endstops and fixed
thermistors, and defines PRINT_START/PRINT_END, so that printer's G-code
prints unchanged. keys.sh prints both keys as shell exports.

  the key form opened; the right key verified; OctoPrint at the Moonraker
  address verified (Moonraker's OctoPrint API); Moonraker at the OctoPrint
  address failed with 404; a closed port failed. No harness check failed.
- A 20 mm cube sliced by the app's command line with the generic Klipper
  profile printed to "complete" on Klipper in about 20 minutes (estimate 10)
  with no shutdowns, and started printing on OctoPrint.

  "Lost communication with MCU 'mcu'"; starting it and restarting klipper
  returns to ready.

The Klipper/Moonraker fake on jusprin-newui-fakeprinter
(tests/printer_sim/fake_moonraker.py) was never on this branch; the docs that
pointed there now point to tests/printer_hosts/README.md.
EOF
